summary:
FlameGap is a Super Intelligence (SI) decision tool that shows where a lunar habitat has experimental evidence of fire safety, where it does not, and which material test should run next.

NASA's reference lunar habitat will breathe 34 % oxygen at 8.2 psia, but no solid-fuel experiment in NASA's PSI archive records more than 22.2 % oxygen. FlameGap bridges that gap with physics: it converts habitat ventilation and lunar buoyancy into one measure, the flame stretch rate, so space station data can be compared with every habitat zone. A physics-informed Gaussian-process model trained on NASA BASS-II data predicts flammability and, crucially, how uncertain it is; zones beyond the evidence are greyed out instead of being called safe. A recommender then ranks the next material tests for FM2 and future flights.

Its key finding: on the Moon, quiet corners are the most flammable places. In a lunar dead zone PMMA can burn at 13.74 % oxygen, almost the microgravity minimum.

Everything is reproducible and verified in two notebooks (88/88 and 17/17 checks), and delivered as an interactive website, an IEEE paper and a 30-second film.
details:
FlameGap is a decision tool that shows where a lunar habitat has experimental evidence of fire safety, where it does not, and which material test should run next.

The problem: NASA's reference lunar Surface Habitat breathes 34 % oxygen at 8.2 psia, and a 2026 NESC assessment found that only 3 of 33 life-support subsystems are acceptable as they are in that atmosphere. Yet no solid-fuel experiment in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive records more than 22.2 % oxygen, and materials are still screened with an upward flame test run in Earth gravity. FM2, the experiment that will burn materials on the Moon, can find the flammability limit of only one material per flight.

How it works: FlameGap converts forced ventilation and lunar buoyancy into one physical measure, the flame stretch rate, so space station tests, Earth tests and habitat zones become comparable. A physics-informed Gaussian-process classifier, trained on 33 points from Table 7.1 of the BASS-II report, predicts whether a flame survives in each habitat zone and, more importantly, how uncertain that prediction is. Its uncertainty grows from 2.54 inside the training data to 9.81 at 34 % O2, and zones beyond the evidence are greyed out instead of being reported as safe. A recommender, S(c) = E(c) · σ(c) · K(c) · (1 − F(c)), ranks which material and condition to test next by combining crew exposure, model uncertainty, closeness to the material's limiting oxygen, and whether FM2 already covers it.

Key finding: on the Moon, quiet corners are the most flammable places. In a lunar dead zone, PMMA can burn at 13.74 % O2, within 0.13 points of the microgravity minimum. On the space station a stagnant corner helps a fire go out; on the Moon it does not.

Benefits and impact: FlameGap lets engineers spend scarce flight tests where the evidence gap is largest, and makes "we have no data here" visible instead of hidden. It supports decisions; it does not replace NASA-STD-6001B.

Tools: Python (NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, SymPy, pypdf) in Google Colab notebooks; React and Vite for an interactive website served by nginx in Docker; LaTeX for an IEEE conference paper; Playwright and FFmpeg to render a 30-second film. Everything is reproducible: a verification notebook passes 88 of 88 checks (source hashes, quotes against the source text, units, symbolic derivations) and a model notebook passes 17 of 17.

Creativity and considerations: I am a software engineer, not a combustion physicist, so I designed the project around honesty about uncertainty: every number traces to a NASA source, every derivation is checked in code, and the model is built to say what it does not know. Limits are stated openly: the model is trained on one fabric and zones use a mean velocity. Team Viva Tiquicia (solo), Cartago, Costa Rica.
